headlines.summary: Follow CNBC's 2026 Technology Executive Council Summit for live updates on AI agents, cybersecurity, AI costs and the future of work.
headlines.article_text: CNBC Technology Summit 2026: AI news and live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu CNBC's Jon Fortt interviews Wikipedia Founder Jimmy Wales at the 2025 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York on October 28, 2025 CNBC At a defining moment for business and technology, artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations operate — and introducing new complexities for the leaders responsible for what comes next. So how are companies adapting and shaping technology's next era — from compute ROI and cybersecurity to regulation and quantum computing? CNBC is convening technology executives, industry experts, and CNBC journalists at the annual Technology Executive Council Summit in New York today to discuss the increasingly central role that technology leaders are playing in this transformation. The TEC Summit is an exclusive event for members; learn more about the TEC and apply for membership at www.cnbccouncils.com/tec . 1 Min Ago Making sure AI is implemented through the lens of the business AI is creating new, fundamentally different operating models for businesses. But often AI engineers are not understanding the business in which they are operating, creating multiple issues when tracking ROI and success of the technology. Nigel Vaz, Publicis Sapient CEO, told CNBC's Jon Fortt that he was at a breakfast before the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit where he met with a group of clients that his firm works with. The CIO of an investment bank that Publicis Sapient works with told Vaz that the bank recently brought in some engineers from Anthropic. "The client said, 'I have 50,000 developers, and they gave me six incredible AI engineers from Anthropic. But they don't understand investment banking. They don't understand the bespoke coding language we use in the bank,'" Vaz said. The client was highlighting something, Vaz said, that he continuously hears which is that people need to think about AI beyond the context of the technology, "because a technology or a tool given to an enterprise is just one part of the problem." "You need some people who understand the context of the business, not in terms of how it operates today, but who have a perspective on how it's going to operate tomorrow because they've got to get somebody from here to there," he said. — Colleen McKown 35 Min Ago The misleading nature of AI's responses In a Wall Street Journal op-ed published in June , Forum AI Founder and CEO Campbell Brown argued that as the world becomes more reliant on AI, there needs to be a more critical lens applied to AI's output. "Already it is so good its mistakes don't look like mistakes," Brown wrote. Speaking with CNBC's Scott Wapner at the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on Wednesday, Brown said the issue remains that "when you read an answer generated by AI, it's presented with such confidence and clarity that it is hard to question it and identify where the mistakes may be." "I think that's what's particularly dangerous," she said. Brown, the former head of global media partnerships at Meta, said this issue is increasingly worrying as people turn to AI for political or election information, and that speaks to how the information is not only presented but where it is sourced. "There's a real critical piece to this that has been somewhat frustrating for me: the labs are not engaging as much as I think they should be with real subject matter expertise," she said. "Human expertise in domains is essential to getting this right." — Ian Thomas 1 Hour Ago The tech-focused discussions at the CNBC WEC Summit CNBC Workforce Executive Council members speak with CNBC's Sharon Epperson at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 27, 2026. CNBC Yesterday, CNBC's Workforce Executive Council held its annual Summit , and the discussion of how human resources professionals help workers adapt to this new AI age was at the top of the agenda. Walmart , the biggest private employer in the world, asked its 2.1 million associates in June that exact question for the first time, trying to get a sense of how one of the most diverse workforces is experiencing AI. What it found, based on more than 1.7 million survey responses, is that while workers have different levels of familiarity and comfort with AI, training and experience with the technology matters. Seventy-seven percent of Walmart's office-based associates said are excited about AI's potential to improve their work, Walmart Chief People Officer for Associate Experience and Digital Maren Waggoner told CNBC's Leslie Picker at the WEC Summit. And as for Walmart's U.S. frontline associates, 84% said they are confident using digital tools, a reflection of the AI-powered tools that many of them are now using in their roles, she said. "We've given them certificates, we've given them training programs and tools, and so they're using it in their day-to-day," Waggoner said. Jill Bruning, chief technology officer of Amentum and a member of the CNBC Technology Executive Council, said at the WEC Summit that strategy should be evolved to be humans in the lead. "There's an AI curve, and we see it. It's going up and it's going fast and has a lot of attributes to it; it's quicker than anything we've seen before," Bruning told CNBC's Susan Caminiti. "So when you think about people on that curve … that gap is getting bigger every day." Bruning said she doesn't know if leadership is adapting fast enough to the technology, and that is creating additional challenges with upskilling as well as what tasks are being delegated to AI. "So your delegation skills are different, and then how do we tell the agents what to do? How do we define that role? She said. "That's human over the loop, not in the loop. We're still in charge." For more from the CNBC WEC Summit, you can see the full live blog here . — Ian Thomas 2 Hours Ago Today's top tech headlines A drone view shows a data center at the Google Storey County Campus in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center in Sparks, Nevada, Oct. 9, 2026. Daniel Cole | Reuters Here are some of the top tech-focused headlines from CNBC this morning: Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips . Google started working on in-house silicon in 2013, but didn't begin selling its tensor processing units (TPUs) to outside customers until the second quarter of this year. Now the company is tapping Oracle's cloud as another avenue for selling TPUs as it tries to bolster competition with Nvidia in the AI chip market. Anthropic’s cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company . Anthropic had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $19.3 billion in short-term investments as of June 30. That exceeded every non-bank U.S. company in CNBC and S&P Capital IQ data except Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet. Amazon’s anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI . Amazon discouraged teams from relying solely on token usage or code generation as measurements of AI adoption, calling them "deeply flawed" metrics in an internal memo. The memo revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI. — Ian Thomas 2 Hours Ago What's on the agenda at this year's TEC Summit Cheng Xin | Getty Images This year's TEC Summit is focusing on what is coming next in AI, whether that's how companies are adapting their strategies based on the advancement in the technology to how they're controlling the costs related to that build out. Discussions will also center on AI regulation, agents, how workers are using the technology and where this acceleration of AI is taking society. headlines.article_text: Google alters cloud playbook turning to partners to sell more AI chips Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Google started working on in-house silicon in 2013, but didn't begin selling its tensor processing units to outside customers until the second quarter of this year. Now the company is tapping Oracle's cloud as another avenue for selling TPUs as it tries to bolster competition with Nvidia in the AI chip market. Thomas Kurian, Google's cloud boss, spent more than 20 years at Oracle before joining Google in 2018. In this article GOOGL ORCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of cloud services at Google LLC, speaks during the Google Cloud Next event in San Francisco on April 9, 2019. Michael Short | Bloomberg | Getty Images Google has spent years pitching customers on the advantage of buying its chips, models and cloud services in one place, offering a full stack that rivals Amazon and Microsoft have tried to replicate. Now, the company is pushing its equipment outside of its own walls to reach more customers and build a bigger business around artificial intelligence chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated. A day ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, Alphabet said Tuesday that Oracle will offer Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, the custom chips the internet giant has been developing since 2013 . It's the first time customers will be able to access TPUs outside of Google's infrastructure, and shows that cloud boss Thomas Kurian, who previously spent more than 20 years at Oracle, is looking elsewhere for growth. "They're a very strong competitor, and it's very possible that they could eventually take market share from Nvidia," said Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, referring to Google's position in chips. Kurian, who joined Google in late 2018, is operating from a position of strength.
